title: Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
description: Your code is deterministic. Claude's output isn't. That changes what 'testing' means.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the difference between testing deterministic code and testing AI-powered features
Identify what parts of a Claude-powered tool can be tested normally vs. need a different approach
Distinguish between testing your code and evaluating prompt quality

contentSections.body: You write a test: call the summarizer, check the output equals a fixed string. It passes today. Tomorrow, Claude phrases the summary slightly differently — same meaning, different words — and your test fails on a tool that isn't actually broken.

### Two different things people call 'testing'

**1. Testing your code** — the parts that are deterministic: does the function parse arguments correctly, does it call the API with the right parameters, does it handle a 429 error, does it write the output file. These behave exactly like testing any other software, because they are.

**2. Evaluating your prompt** — the parts that involve Claude's actual output: is the summary accurate, is the tone right, did it follow the format instruction. These can't use `===` because the output varies between runs even with identical input.

Mixing these two up is the most common mistake — trying to unit-test prompt quality with exact-match assertions, or skipping code testing because 'it's AI, you can't test it.'

contentSections.question: Your CLI tool has a bug: it crashes with 'undefined is not a function' whenever the input file is empty. Is this a code bug or a prompt quality issue?
contentSections.answer: **A code bug.** Crashing on empty input has nothing to do with what Claude generates — it's a missing input validation check in your own code, and it's fully deterministic and testable with a normal unit test: pass an empty string, assert it doesn't throw.
contentSections.hint: Would this bug happen no matter what Claude's response was?

contentSections.body: Test your code's logic with normal assertions. Evaluate Claude's output quality with a different method — you'll build that method in this module.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how to test your CLI summarizer tool.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in a normal unit test (exact assertions), not an evaluation?

items.label: Does --model haiku set the right value?
Does empty input produce a clear error, not a crash?
Does a 429 response trigger a retry, not a crash?
Does the output file get written with the right content?

explanation.arg-parsing: Unit test — the expected value is exact and known before running.
explanation.input-validation: Unit test — the expected error behavior is exact and known.
explanation.error-handling: Unit test — the expected retry behavior is exact and known.
explanation.file-io: Unit test — the expected file content is exact and known.
explanation.accuracy: Evaluation — accuracy can't use === because the exact wording varies between runs even with identical input.
explanation.tone: Evaluation — 'appropriate tone' can't be checked with an exact-match assertion.

contentSections.synthesis: If you can write down the exact expected output before running the code, it's a unit test. If the 'correct' answer could reasonably vary in wording, it's an evaluation. Mixing these up is the most common mistake — trying to unit-test prompt quality with exact-match assertions, or skipping code testing because 'it's AI, you can't test it.'

contentSections.body:
A practical split for a typical CLI tool:

```
✓ Unit test (normal, exact assertions):
  - Argument parsing (does --model haiku set the right value?)
  - Input validation (does empty input produce a clear error, not a crash?)
  - Error handling (does a 429 response trigger a retry, not a crash?)
  - File I/O (does the output file get written with the right content?)

✓ Evaluation (approximate, quality-based — covered later in this module):
  - Is the summary actually accurate?
  - Did the output follow the requested format?
  - Is the tone appropriate?
```

As a rule: if you can write down the exact expected output before running the code, it's a unit test. If the 'correct' answer could reasonably vary in wording, it's an evaluation.

**Start with the unit-testable half.** Most bugs reported by real users of AI tools turn out to be ordinary code bugs — a missing null check, an unhandled error status — not the AI 'being wrong.' Fixing the boring half first removes most of your bug reports.

title: Mocking Claude in Tests
description: Test your tool's logic without spending money or waiting on the real API every run.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why calling the real API in every test run is a bad practice
Write a mock Claude client that returns fixed responses
Structure code to make mocking possible (dependency injection)

contentSections.title: Why not just call the real API in tests?

contentSections.body: You run your test suite 20 times while debugging a small change. Each run makes a real API call. That's 20 charges for a bug fix that has nothing to do with what Claude says — and your tests are now slow, cost money, and can fail because of a network hiccup instead of an actual bug.

contentSections.question: What's the one change that made the second `summarize` function testable, when the first one wasn't?
contentSections.answer: **The client became a parameter instead of being created inside the function.** This is dependency injection — the function no longer decides how to get its dependencies, the caller does. That single change is what lets a test substitute a fake client without touching the function's internals.
contentSections.hint: Compare where `new Anthropic()` appears in each version.

contentSections.body: Pass dependencies in as parameters instead of creating them inside a function. That one pattern makes almost anything mockable.

contentSections.question: This function is hard to unit test. What's the flaw?

options.label: The Claude client is created inside the function, so a test can't swap in a fake one

feedback.flaw: Right — the client is baked in. There's no way to pass a mock client without editing the function itself.
feedback.fine: It reads cleanly, but that's exactly the problem — there's no seam for a test to inject a fake client, so every test call becomes a real, billed API call.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Instead of creating the Claude client inside the function, pass it in as a parameter. Then tests can pass a fake one — neither test makes a real API call, both run in milliseconds and cost nothing.

contentSections.body: **Mocked tests don't catch prompt quality problems.** A mock always returns whatever you told it to — it can't tell you if your real prompt produces bad summaries. That's what evaluation, covered later in this module, is for.

title: Debugging Bad Output
description: Your tool returned something wrong. Is it the prompt, the code, or the input? A method for finding out.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a systematic method to isolate whether a bug is in code, prompt, or input
Use verbose logging to capture the exact prompt and response for debugging
Diagnose a specific failing example and identify the root cause

contentSections.title: Three places a bug can hide

contentSections.body: Your summarizer just returned three sentences about a topic that isn't in the document you fed it. Before you touch the system prompt, you need to know: did the wrong text actually reach Claude in the first place?

### The isolation method

When output is wrong, check in this order — each step rules out one whole category of cause:

**1. Check what actually reached Claude.** Log the exact prompt sent, not what you think you sent. A file-reading bug, an encoding issue, or a truncated string upstream is a code bug wearing a prompt-quality costume.

**2. Check what Claude actually returned, raw.** Before your code parses or reformats the response, log it unmodified. Sometimes the model's raw answer was fine and your parsing logic broke it.

**3. Only then, question the prompt itself.** If the input was correct and the raw output is still wrong, that's a genuine prompt problem — the instructions are ambiguous, missing context, or asking for something Claude can't reliably do.

contentSections.question: A user reports your tool summarized the wrong document entirely. You check the logs and see the raw prompt sent to Claude contained text from a completely different file. Where's the bug?
contentSections.answer: **In your code, before the API call — likely file-reading or path-handling logic.** The prompt sent was already wrong, so nothing about the model's behavior is at fault here. No amount of prompt tweaking would fix a bug that happens before the prompt is even built.
contentSections.hint: At which step in the isolation method did this bug become visible?

contentSections.body: Log the exact prompt sent and the exact raw response received, before assuming the problem is prompt quality. Most 'AI is wrong' bug reports turn out to be upstream code bugs.

contentSections.question: Put these debugging steps in order when output looks wrong.
steps: Check what actually reached Claude — log the exact prompt sent
Check what Claude actually returned, raw, before your code parses it
Only then, question the prompt itself
contentSections.explanation: Each step rules out one whole category of cause. A file-reading bug, an encoding issue, or a truncated string upstream is a code bug wearing a prompt-quality costume — checking the actual prompt sent first catches this before you waste time rewriting instructions that were never the real problem.

contentSections.body: **Keep a small folder of known-bad examples.** Every time a real bug surfaces, save the input that triggered it. This becomes the seed for the eval harness you'll build in this module's last lesson — a way to make sure old bugs don't come back.

title: Handling Edge Cases
description: Empty input, giant input, non-English input. The cases that don't show up until real users arrive.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the common edge cases that break AI-powered tools
Write input validation that catches edge cases before they reach the API
Handle a too-large input by chunking or truncating with a clear warning

contentSections.title: The inputs you didn't think to test

contentSections.body: Your summarizer works perfectly in every demo. Then a real user pastes in an empty clipboard, another pastes a 40,000-word document, and a third pastes text in a language you never tested. None of these are unusual for real usage — they're just inputs you never happened to try.

### The edge cases that actually happen

1. **Empty input** — user hits submit with nothing typed. Should produce a clear message, not a confusing API call with blank content.
2. **Input larger than the context window** — a full book pasted into a tool meant for short documents. Needs chunking or a clear size limit, not a silent failure.
3. **Input in an unexpected language** — your prompt says 'summarize in English' but never says what to do if the input isn't English.
4. **Input that's mostly whitespace or garbage** — a pasted screenshot's OCR text, or an accidental paste of binary data.
5. **Special characters that break your code, not Claude** — quotes, newlines, or unicode that trips up string handling before the API call even happens.

None of these are rare in production. They're just absent from a happy-path demo.

contentSections.question: A user pastes a 200-page PDF's worth of text into your summarizer, which is meant for single-page documents. What's the better failure mode: silently truncating the input, or rejecting it with a message?
contentSections.answer: **Reject it with a specific message** — 'This tool handles documents up to about 2,000 words. Yours is 40,000 words — try summarizing it in sections.' Silent truncation produces a summary that looks complete but is actually based on a fraction of the document, which is more misleading than an honest refusal.
contentSections.hint: Which failure mode is more honest about what actually happened?

contentSections.body: An honest rejection beats a silent partial result. If your tool can't handle an input properly, say so — don't quietly do a worse job and let the user assume it worked.

contentSections.scenario: You're testing your summarizer tool against real-world inputs, not just demo-happy-path text.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real edge cases the lesson calls out?

items.label: Empty input — user hits submit with nothing typed
Input larger than the context window — a full book pasted in
Input that's mostly whitespace or garbage, like OCR text
Special characters that break your code, not Claude
The user's internet connection is slow
The user's system clock is in the wrong timezone

explanation.empty: Real edge case — should produce a clear message, not a confusing API call with blank content.
explanation.oversized: Real edge case — needs chunking or a clear size limit, not a silent failure.
explanation.wrong-lang: Real edge case — your prompt may say 'summarize in English' but never say what to do if the input isn't.
explanation.garbage: Real edge case — a pasted screenshot's OCR text or accidental binary paste.
explanation.special-chars: Real edge case — quotes, newlines, or unicode that trips up string handling before the API call even happens.
explanation.slow-network: A real issue in general, but not one of the input edge cases this lesson covers.
explanation.wrong-timezone: A real issue in general, but not one of the input edge cases this lesson covers.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these are rare in production. They're just absent from a happy-path demo.

contentSections.body: **Chunking, when you do need to handle long input:** split into sections under the word limit, summarize each with a single API call, then run one final call that summarizes the summaries. It costs more per document but handles genuinely long input honestly.

title: Building an Eval Harness
description: A small script that checks your prompt still works before you ship a change to it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what an eval harness is and why prompt changes need one
Build a script that runs a set of test cases against a prompt and reports pass/fail
Design evaluation criteria for a specific tool's output quality

contentSections.title: Why prompt changes need their own test suite

contentSections.body: You tweak your system prompt to fix a formatting issue on one example. It works. You ship it. Two days later a user reports the tool now ignores half their document — a case your one manual check never covered.

contentSections.scenario: You tweak your system prompt to fix a formatting issue on one example. It works. You ship it. Two days later a user reports the tool now ignores half their document — a case your one manual check never covered.
contentSections.question: What would have caught this before shipping?

options.label: Testing the one example you were fixing more carefully
An eval harness — a set of representative cases run automatically on every prompt change

feedback.eval-harness: Right — a single manual check, however careful, only covers the one case you're looking at. An eval harness runs a whole representative set automatically, including known-bad examples from earlier debugging, every time you change the prompt.
feedback.retest-one: Retesting the same one example wouldn't have caught this — the regression showed up on a different case (long documents) that your one-off check never covered.

contentSections.mechanism: A small collection of representative inputs, paired with criteria for what a good output looks like, run automatically every time you change your prompt — not a single test, a set, covering the range of real inputs your tool sees, including the known-bad examples you've been saving from earlier debugging sessions.

contentSections.body:
### What an eval harness is

A small collection of representative inputs, paired with criteria for what a good output looks like, run automatically every time you change your prompt. Not a single test — a set, covering the range of real inputs your tool sees, including the known-bad examples you've been saving from earlier debugging sessions.

```js
// eval-cases.json
[
  { "id": "short-doc", "input": "...", "mustContain": ["key term X"], "maxWords": 60 },
  { "id": "long-doc", "input": "...", "mustContain": ["key term Y"], "maxWords": 80 },
  { "id": "known-bug-01", "input": "...", "mustContain": ["correct topic"], "mustNotContain": ["wrong topic that leaked in before"] }
]
```

Each case has automatable checks — word count limits, required or forbidden terms — even though the full output can't be checked with exact equality.

contentSections.question: Why include a 'known-bug-01' case that specifically checks for a bug you already fixed?
contentSections.answer: **Regression prevention.** Prompt changes can silently reintroduce old bugs — a wording tweak meant to fix one thing can accidentally undo the fix for another. A case built from a real past failure catches this automatically, instead of relying on someone remembering to manually re-check every old bug every time the prompt changes.
contentSections.hint: What happens six months from now when someone else edits this prompt without knowing the tool's history?

contentSections.body: An eval harness turns 'I checked one example and it looked fine' into 'I ran 15 representative cases and they all passed' — the difference between a hope and a check.

**Start with 5-10 cases, not 50.** A small harness you actually run beats a comprehensive one you never finish building. Add a new case every time a real bug surfaces — the harness grows exactly where your tool has actually failed before.
